final_answer:
MEMORANDUM (privileged draft)
RE: ClinAssist AI - AI disclosure comparison across jurisdictions and prioritized remediation
Today is 2 October 2026, so the record is about 15 months stale; Phase 1 (Q1 2026) should already have occurred. Confirm what has actually gone live.

1. BOTTOM LINE
(a) The consent form fails everywhere. All sources agree. Its one-sentence technology paragraph says nothing about AI. Section 3 also states that no tool "operates independently of physician oversight", which the tech spec contradicts (s.4, 6.2: ClinAssist writes risk scores and ICD-10 codes into the chart without physician approval). Neither law firm flagged this. It is an affirmative misstatement, not just an omission, and creates deception exposure (e.g., Mass. c. 93A, which S&C itself cites). Fix it first.
(b) The binding constraint is engineering, not drafting. The tech spec (s.4.3, 6.3, 8.3-8.4) says there is no patient-level opt-out, no jurisdiction toggle, and auto-population cannot be disabled. The only lever is disabling the whole facility. A patient-level bypass is feasible but needs 4-6 months, is unbudgeted, and likely needs a 510(k) supplement. S&C's December 2025 "configurable" target is infeasible on the documented roadmap. Every opt-out or opt-in regime (Washington; Texas per tracker; Maryland, Oregon and Illinois SB 2243 per sources; Netherlands) depends on this feature.
(c) The sources conflict materially, and I could not resolve the conflicts from the record. The tracker disagrees with both outside analyses on effective dates, content, penalties, and even which statutes exist. Independent checks I ran contradict several state citations (see 5). No state-law conclusion below should drive deployment until primary statutory text is pulled.

2. HOW THE SOURCES CONFLICT (reconciled where possible)
Effective dates: Connecticut - S&C/Halberd 3/1/26 vs tracker 10/1/25. Virginia - 1/1/26 vs 7/1/26. Minnesota - 4/1/26 vs 8/1/26. Washington - 1/1/26 (Phase 2) vs tracker 1/1/27 (Phase 3). Phasing also differs: tracker Phase 2 has 6 hospitals and Phase 3 has 5 facilities (23 total), against 12/8/18+3 in the tech spec, Halberd and S&C. The tech spec is the controlling internal source for deployment scope.
Content: Illinois HB 3773 - S&C/Halberd: point-of-care disclosure plus chart documentation, private right of action; tracker: prior written notice, patient acknowledgment, 7-year retention, emergency exception, no private action. Texas HB 2100 - S&C/Halberd: plain-language disclosure before or with diagnosis, AG only, no stated penalty; tracker: AI-use disclosure plus option to request non-AI diagnosis (feasibility exception), EHR notation, $5,000. Connecticut - public documentation (memos) vs oversight committee and annual DPH report (tracker). Maryland - written consent (S&C reading of operative text) vs "disclosure" (Halberd, tracker); Oregon - registration and impact assessment (memos) vs informed consent and public audit (tracker); New York AB 5691 - portal badge vs verbal and written disclosure, accountability officer, proposed private action.
Statutes missing from both firm analyses but in the tracker: California AB 2930 (pre-deployment published impact assessment, eff. 1/1/26, $15,000); Illinois SB 2243 (written consent before AI processes health data, BIPA-style private action, 3-year retention, deletion right); Texas SB 940 (AI processing records, patient log access); New York SB 7503 (pending bias audit). If SB 2243 is as described, Illinois is a consent state, not disclosure-only, and Phase 1 cannot proceed there without the bypass. Treat as highest-priority verification item.
Exemptions: Halberd says Minnesota (FDA CDS carve-out) and Virginia (administrative-task exemption) fully exempt ClinAssist. S&C says no. The tech spec sides with S&C on the facts: s.3.2 ("clinical functions - not administrative tasks"; no scheduling, billing or coding for reimbursement) and s.4.3 (system is "not merely providing information to a licensed practitioner who independently exercises clinical judgment"). Halberd also quotes the Minnesota carve-out without the second prong that S&C quotes. Conclusion: do not rely on either exemption; plan full compliance.
Exposure: S&C's ">$13 billion" does not follow from its own components ($6.3B + $6.2B = $12.5B; plus $351M = $12.85B). Halberd's realistic range of $45-120M is internally inconsistent: California $63M plus Illinois $62M (tracker) already exceeds $120M before Texas, Colorado, EU or any private litigation, and it excludes Minnesota/Virginia on the exemptions I reject. S&C's "$819M" EU exposure is wrong for Art. 26/27/50 breaches (see 4).
Language: S&C places the 23% Spanish figure at California facilities; Choi's email shows it is network-wide and the two California hospitals are 34%. Choi says Illinois has language-access provisions; S&C says none (relying on Title VI). Unresolved. 
Impact assessments: S&C overstates the Halberd disagreement; Halberd s.7.2 also proposes a core document with jurisdiction addenda. Real differences: Halberd says Colorado's assessment is produced to the AG on request, not public; S&C says a public summary is required. Recommendation common to both: a shared core with separate jurisdiction-specific deliverables (Colorado, California AB 2930, Connecticut documentation, Oregon filing if enacted, any EU assessment), one owner.

3. U.S. COMPARISON (disclosure vs consent; timing; opt-out)
Phase 1. Massachusetts: no AI statute. California SB 1047 : notice, plain-language role, right to human review; timing unspecified; Civil Code 1632 translation; plus AB 2930 assessment. Texas: before or concurrent with diagnosis (per memos); tracker adds non-AI option. Illinois: point of care / prior notice, chart record; SB 2243 consent. Colorado: notice and annual assessment (see 5 on date). New York: pending. 
Phase 2. Connecticut: public documentation plus individual disclosure. Virginia, Minnesota: full disclosure. Washington: named-system disclosure plus patient right to non-AI evaluation (opt-out). Maryland: consent if enacted. Oregon: pending. NJ, Georgia: no statute; best-practice disclosure.
Timing: auto-population fires at encounter creation (tech spec s.6.3), before any clinician sees the patient. Early-trigger regimes (Washington, Colorado; Texas "before") are engaged at registration; Illinois "point of care" is ambiguous. S&C's two-stage disclosure (written at intake, confirmed at encounter) is the sound answer; it cannot cure opt-out or consent regimes, because processing has already occurred by then.

4. EU COMPARISON AND ERRORS IN THE EU WORK
Hierarchy: EU AI Act and GDPR are binding; CNIL, Dutch AP and German BMG materials are guidance. The tracker calls CNIL guidance "binding" and S&C says Meridian "must comply" with the AP position, but the EU briefing calls it non-binding. Plan for AP expectations; seek local counsel.
Errors to correct (searches against published Article 50 commentary and the Commission service desk):
- Article 50(4) concerns deepfakes and public-interest text. Emotion recognition and biometric categorization are Art. 50(3). Both EU documents mislabel it, and both recommend "precautionary" 50(4) disclosures because vitals and imaging are "biometric-adjacent". The tech spec (s.2.2, 5.3, 7.4) states the system does no emotion recognition, no biometric categorization, and no audio or video. Vitals and imaging are not biometric data used for categorization. Drop this workstream.
- Annex III point 5(a) concerns eligibility for essential public benefits, not medical diagnosis; all documents mischaracterize it. ClinAssist's high-risk status most plausibly arises under Art. 6(1)/Annex I (medical device needing notified-body assessment), consistent with the pending MDR conformity assessment (spec s.7.4). Consequences: the Annex III-specific patient-notice duty (Art. 26(11)) and Art. 27 FRIA may not attach; high-risk application dates differ. EU counsel should confirm (primary text not retrieved).
- Dates are wrong in every document. Art. 50 applies from 2 August 2026, not 2025. The Digital Omnibus (reported in force 27 July 2026) moved Annex III high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027 and Annex I to 2 August 2028, left Art. 50 dates intact, and gave existing systems until 2 December 2026 for Art. 50(2) marking. Secondary-source reports; confirm in the Official Journal.
- Art. 50(1)-(2) allocate duties to providers (interaction notice, machine-readable marking), not a general patient notice by deployers. The documents' "Art. 50(2) patient notice" is therefore doubtful; the reliable patient-notice basis is GDPR Arts. 12-14 (and 13(2)(f)/15(1)(h) for automated decisions).
- Provider status: the tech spec says Meridian developed and owns ClinAssist (Clearpoint built the engine under an MSA). Meridian may be the "provider"/manufacturer, with conformity, CE-marking and documentation duties, not just a deployer. Both EU documents assume deployer-only. MDR conformity is a Phase 3 gating item.
- Penalties: the 7%/EUR 35M tier covers prohibited practices only. Deployer and provider high-risk duties (Arts. 16-27) and Art. 50 sit at EUR 15M or 3% (about $351M on $11.7B turnover). GDPR Art. 9/22 infringements carry up to 4% (about $468M) cumulatively.
Member states: Germany - German-language disclosure; draft BMG guidance (CE status/conformity summary; tracker adds written notice, naming system in records, recommended physician co-signature), not final. France - GDPR Art. 22 risk heightened by auto-population before review; S&C sees no explicit-consent layer, tracker says CNIL requires Art. 9 consent: unresolved, so plan for explicit consent as fallback. Art. 22 analysis should also consider the CJEU's SCHUFA ruling (C-634/21, from memory, not retrieved) that a score can itself be the "decision". Netherlands - AP position of explicit consent under Art. 9(2)(a) (arguably in tension with Art. 9(2)(h)); requires a non-AI pathway, so it needs the bypass.

5. CURRENCY AND VERIFICATION FLAGS
My checks: California SB 1047 (2024) was the frontier-model safety bill, vetoed 29 Sept 2024; California's actual health-AI disclosure law is AB 3030 (generative AI patient communications, eff. 1/1/25). Illinois HB 3773 is the Human Rights Act employment-AI amendment (signed 8/9/24, eff. 1/1/26). Texas's AI-diagnosis disclosure law found was SB 1188 (eff. 9/1/25; $5,000-$250,000 penalties); I found no matching HB 2100. Colorado SB 24-205 was delayed to 30 June 2026 and, per search reports, replaced by SB 26-189 effective 1 January 2027. The matter documents' descriptions of these statutes therefore cannot be assumed accurate.

6. PRIORITIZED REMEDIATION
P0 - immediately (gating):
1. Pull primary text and current status for every statute, bill and guidance document in the tracker (priority: IL SB 2243, TX opt-out and EHR duties, CA AB 2930, Colorado replacement, MN/VA exemption text, MD SB 818). Replace the tracker as source of record.
2. Confirm whether any live-patient processing has occurred at CA, TX or IL sites since 1 July 2025 / 1 September 2025 / 1 January 2026. If so, run a privileged audit and consider remediation; if not, keep the hold .
3. Withdraw and replace the consent paragraph immediately; stop using the "no tool operates independently" sentence.
4. Decide and fund the patient-level bypass and jurisdiction profiles (4-6 months plus 510(k) supplement assessment with FDA counsel). Until validated, do not go live in Washington, the Netherlands, Maryland (if enacted), Illinois (if consent applies), or any jurisdiction with a patient opt-out. Facility-level disablement is the interim option.
5. Brief the board that compliance, not investor timing (Arbor Ridge email 6/10/25), sets go-live; consider NYSE disclosure implications.
P1 - before any live use in Phase 1 states:
6. Modular disclosure framework: common core naming ClinAssist AI, its role, data analyzed, auto-population, human review right; state supplements; two-stage delivery.
7. Illinois EHR notation field (date, time, method; retention per verified statute) and Texas EHR notation.
8. Translation: Spanish and Mandarin first (California hospitals 34% Spanish), then other languages; resolve Illinois language-access question.
9. California AB 2930 assessment, Colorado assessment under whatever law now governs; designate one owner; separate deliverables.
P2 - before Phase 2:
10. Washington opt-out workflow; Minnesota and Virginia full disclosure (no exemption reliance); Connecticut public documentation and, if the tracker is right, oversight committee and DPH report; Minnesota validation-data summary.
11. Contingency plans for Maryland consent and Oregon; New York badge in portal design.
12. Correct internal tracker classifications (Maryland as consent).
P3 - before Phase 3 (Q1 2027, now close):
13. Confirm MDR/CE conformity and Meridian's provider-or-deployer role; amend Clearpoint MSA flow-downs.
14. EU counsel to re-base the analysis on correct AI Act articles and dates; drop Art. 50(4) work; FRIA only if counsel confirms it applies; commission GDPR DPIA and Art. 22 assessment (Lyon, with affirmative-confirmation workflow and override audit logs).
15. Local-language GDPR Arts. 12-14 notices; Rotterdam separate explicit-consent protocol and non-AI pathway; monitor German guidance finalization.

7. UNRESOLVED
State statute content and dates; whether Illinois has a private action and consent rule; Texas penalty and opt-out; Colorado current regime; EU Annex I classification and Art. 27 applicability; France Art. 9 consent; CNIL/AP status; whether Phase 1 launched; FDA view on bypass change. Statutory text was not retrieved for any state law.
